asm:segment:general_public:cold.what: share of local cold burden in general_public

asm:segment:general_public:heat.what: share of local heat burden in general_public

asm:segment:households_without_adequate_.what: share of local cold burden in households_without_adequate_heat
asm:segment:households_without_adequate_.basis: ASSUMPTION carried from the Phoenix file

asm:segment:low_income:cold.what: share of local cold burden in low_income
asm:segment:low_income:cold.basis: Base as above. Multiplier: Burke, Wilson et al. 2026 - energy prices raise winter mortality; UK Winter Fuel Payment reduced cold mortality (direction cited); 1.5 ASSUMPTION

asm:segment:low_income:heat.what: share of local heat burden in low_income
asm:segment:low_income:heat.basis: Base: ACS 2019-23 B17001 share below poverty. Multiplier: Burke, Wilson et al. 2026 - income support (minimum wage, cash transfers) reduces heat mortality, i.e. low income raises vulnerability (direction cited); 1.5 ASSUMPTION

asm:segment:mental_illness_or_substance_.what: share of local heat burden in mental_illness_or_substance_use
asm:segment:mental_illness_or_substance_.basis: Coded part: ~25% of CA death certificates listing heat-related illness (2018-2022) also list drug overdose (CDC data reported by KFF Health News / California Healthline, 2023). Uncoded part: population share 0.05 ASSUMPTION x 2.0 ASSUMPTION

asm:segment:older_adults:cold.what: share of local cold burden in older_adults
asm:segment:older_adults:cold.basis: Base as above. Multiplier: Burke, Wilson et al. 2026 sec.3 - relative cold risk rises with age (direction cited); 1.1 is ASSUMPTION; capped so share <= 1 | base: state value used as proxy (ASSUMPTION)

asm:segment:older_adults:heat.what: share of local heat burden in older_adults
asm:segment:older_adults:heat.basis: Base: CDPH final death profiles, residence, all causes, 2018/2019/2023/2024 (65+ = share of deaths). Multiplier: Burke, Wilson et al. 2026 sec.3 - relative heat risk falls with age but higher baseline mortality offsets it (direction cited); 0.8 is ASSUMPTION | base: state value used as proxy (ASSUMPTION)

asm:segment:outage_exposed:heat.what: share of local heat burden in outage_exposed
asm:segment:outage_exposed:heat.basis: ASSUMPTION carried from the Phoenix file; Burke et al.: outages raise hot-day mortality impact 61%/hour above 80F

asm:segment:outdoor_workers:heat.what: share of local heat burden in outdoor_workers
asm:segment:outdoor_workers:heat.basis: Base: ACS 2019-23 C24010 natural resources/construction/maintenance share of employed x employment-to-population 0.47 (ASSUMPTION). Multiplier 1.0 ASSUMPTION (high exposure offset by low working-age baseline mortality)

asm:segment:people_experiencing_homeless.what: share of local cold burden in people_experiencing_homelessness
asm:segment:people_experiencing_homeless.basis: PIT 2024 population share x all-cause mortality ratio 3.0 ASSUMPTION (hypothermia deaths rising among older unhoused people: KFF Health News 2024) | base: state value used as proxy (ASSUMPTION)

asm:segment:people_experiencing_homeless.what: share of local heat burden in people_experiencing_homelessness
asm:segment:people_experiencing_homeless.basis: Coded part: ~13% of CA hospitalizations with primary heat-related-illness diagnosis 2017-2021 were homeless (state data reported by KFF Health News / California Healthline, 2023). Uncoded part: PIT 2024 (HUD, CA CoCs) population share x all-cause mortality ratio 3.0 ASSUMPTION. Coded fraction of attributable heat deaths = trigger_fallbacks f_coded | base: state value used as proxy (ASSUMPTION)

asm:segment:recreational_outdoor_users:h.what: share of local heat burden in recreational_outdoor_users
asm:segment:recreational_outdoor_users:h.basis: ASSUMPTION carried from the Phoenix file

asm:segment:renters_or_housing_insecure:.what: share of local heat burden in renters_or_housing_insecure
asm:segment:renters_or_housing_insecure:.basis: Base: ACS 2019-23 B25003 renter-occupied share of households. Multiplier 0.6 ASSUMPTION: cooling standards reach only renters with inadequate cooling

asm:segment:severe_acute_heat_illness_ca.what: share of local heat burden in severe_acute_heat_illness_cases
asm:segment:severe_acute_heat_illness_ca.basis: f_coded x 0.3 (ASSUMPTION: share of coded-type cases reaching EMS alive; Phoenix file used the same 0.3)

calc:agnostic:floor.label: deaths averted per year by the inherited (county and state) plans' firm measures, as written
calc:agnostic:floor.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_inherited measures (1 − segment_share × coverage × effect × active))

calc:agnostic:plan.label: deaths averted per year by the plan's firm measures
calc:agnostic:plan.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_measures (1 − segment_share × coverage × effect × active))

calc:agnostic:plan_all.label: deaths averted per year by all the plan's firm measures, standing commitments included
calc:agnostic:plan_all.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_measures (1 − segment_share × coverage × effect × active)), every firm measure

calc:agnostic:portfolio.label: deaths averted per year by the mix shown (recomputed by the app for the strategies, thresholds and coverage you set)
calc:agnostic:portfolio.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_options (1 − min(1, segment_share × coverage × m) × effect × active)); cost = tier cost × m; at most one threshold per strategy; best mix = multi-start greedy + Pareto filter (pipeline/portfolio.py)

calc:agnostic:residents_best.label: best mix of the stack's measures and the shared menu at the stack's own total cost
calc:agnostic:residents_best.formula: max over a multi-start greedy frontier (stack measures at any timing + shared menu) with cost ≤ stack cost

calc:agnostic:residents_plan.label: deaths averted per year by every plan in the stack (inherited + own), as written
calc:agnostic:residents_plan.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_stack measures (1 − r × active))

calc:agnostic:vintage_2025.label: deaths averted per year by the jurisdiction's own plans in force in 2025, as written, on today's floor, harm and evidence
calc:agnostic:vintage_2025.formula: Σ_days residual_deaths_day × (1 − Π_measures (1 − r × active)), measures from the documents in force that year

ev:EV01.finding: Three US studies find limited or uncertain mortality effects of heat alerts. Korea: all-cause mortality rose on alert days (decreases for some groups). Japan: ambulance transports rose. Shenzhen: ~10% less heat illness. Germany: no mortality effect. Spain: ~7% fewer hot-day workplace injuries after lowering alert thresholds. Paper concludes alerts alone are insufficient.
ev:EV01.notes: Harmful estimate exists (Korea); keep negative lower bound.
ev:EV01.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV02.finding: No causal health evaluation of cold alerts alone identified (winter forecast lead time reduced car crashes, coded under forecasts).
ev:EV02.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV04.finding: Pakistan RCT: no mortality effect but 38% fewer unscheduled hospital visits. India program: ~41% fewer heat-stroke deaths. China: ~20% less heat illness (not significant). Australia RCT: more protective behavior, less self-reported heat stress. Outdoor worker RCT: non-significant.
ev:EV04.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV05.finding: Paper flags targeted cold information as a critical research priority; no causal studies.
ev:EV05.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV09.finding: California standard: 87% reduction in hot-day injury effect and 33% fewer outdoor-worker heat deaths (neither significant). Dallas rest-break ordinance: no significant effect. El Salvador water/rest: better kidney function (imprecise).
ev:EV09.notes: Applies to worker population only, not whole-population burden.
ev:EV09.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV10.finding: No randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation of cooling centers on health identified.
ev:EV10.notes: Very common in plans; key 'popular but unproven' case.
ev:EV10.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV11.finding: US multifamily and Tennessee weatherization: better comfort/self-reported health, imprecise. New Zealand insulation: 11% fewer all-cause, 15% fewer respiratory admissions; related RCT 47% fewer respiratory admissions (not significant). Wales: no clear benefit. East Germany retrofits: 2.9% fewer circulatory hospitalizations 65+, concentrated on coldest days.
ev:EV11.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV13.finding: US: doubling home-heating prices raised winter all-cause mortality ~2%. Japan: higher residential energy prices raised mortality on days below 0C. New Zealand: higher electricity prices raised asthma admissions. China subsidized heating: ~50% lower cold-related mortality. UK Winter Fuel Payment RD: no individual health effect (DiD result coded under income).
ev:EV13.notes: Paper: reducing heating cost reduces cold harm; LIHEAP evaluation is an open research need.
ev:EV13.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV14.finding: Paper notes no evidence on heat for affordability programs.
ev:EV14.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV15.finding: US: each additional outage hour on a day above 80F raised that day's mortality impact by 61%. Australia: outages nearly doubled the effect of extreme heat on ambulance attendances.
ev:EV15.notes: Evidence is on harm of outages, not on a specific reliability program; effect band is a team assumption about avoidable outage-attributable share.
ev:EV15.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV19.finding: Disconnections rise during extreme heat and fall on vulnerable groups; moratoria reduce disconnections; no direct causal health evaluation.
ev:EV19.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV20.finding: AC ownership correlates with lower heat mortality but programs promoting AC lack causal health evaluation; low-income US households run AC less. German hospital RCT: radiant cooling cut respiratory patients' stay by one third.
ev:EV20.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV21.finding: New Zealand RCT: non-polluting heaters raised indoor temps and cut child asthma doctor visits ~30%.
ev:EV21.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV25.finding: US community health center expansion: ~14% lower heat-related mortality. India community health workers: ~10% lower hot-day infant mortality. India mental health services reduced heat-related mental health harm.
ev:EV25.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV26.finding: US hospital desegregation (acute care access) nearly eliminated cold effect on Black infant mortality; community health centers showed no cold effect.
ev:EV26.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV27.finding: Mexico coverage expansion: 36% smaller moderate-cold mortality effect. Colombia: ~55% smaller cold mortality effect.
ev:EV27.notes: No US study; transport with caution.
ev:EV27.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV28.finding: Same studies: unclear effects for heat.
ev:EV28.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV29.finding: No causal evaluations; Mexico evidence shows heat-driven hospital congestion worsens outcomes, suggesting plausibility.
ev:EV29.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV35.finding: Closest reviewed evidence: targeted info campaigns; untargeted versions not evaluated.
ev:EV35.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV36.finding: Closest reviewed evidence: Toronto cold program (null).
ev:EV36.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV37.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV38.finding: Closest reviewed evidence: targeted info campaigns (promising, non-US).
ev:EV38.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

plan:48201_HMP_2025_C02.page_text:
2025 Harris County Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan Mitigation Strategy
Area Wide Action #2 (AW_2)
Action Description Continue to maintain and update the hazard mitigation page on
HCOHSEM’s ReadyHarris website with relevant information on the
plan’s implementation, such as annual progress reports, public
comment opportunities, and plan integration opportunities. Each

Description of the Problem: Without a well-maintained online resource and coordination among
planning partners, important updates and opportunities for
involvement risk being overlooked, limiting community awareness
and collaboration in hazard mitigation efforts.
Description of the Solution: This provides a centralized, continuously updated online resource
that keeps the public and stakeholders informed about the progress
and implementation of the hazard mitigation plan. By sharing annual
reports and avenues for public involvement, it promotes
transparency, engagement, and collaboration.

plan:48201_HMP_2025_C05.page_text:
2025 Harris County Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan Mitigation Strategy
Area Wide Action 5 (AW_5)
Action Description Continue to develop, improve and implement an enhanced mass
public warning and alert system (iPAWS) within the Regional Joint
Information Center to provide warning capability throughout Harris
County to support the emergency management of all hazards of
concern and disasters impacting critical infrastructure and residents
Lead Agency: Harris County Office of Homeland Security & Emergency
Management
Supporting Agencies: All Planning Partners
Hazard(s) of Concern: Coastal Erosion, Dam/Levee Failure, Drought, Earthquake, Extreme
Cold, Extreme Heat, Flooding, Hurricanes/Coastal Storms, Mass
Movement, Severe Weather, Tsunami, Wildfire, Energy Pipeline
Failures, Public Health Emergency, Technology Failure, Toxic
Release/HazMat, Utilities Failure
Description of the Problem: Without a robust and reliable mass public warning system, timely
communication during hazard events can be compromised, putting
lives and property at greater risk.
Description of the Solution: By expanding and strengthening this mass notification capability,
the County can quickly disseminate critical warnings and information
to residents, improving emergency response and public safety
across all hazards of concern.
Estimated Cost: Low (<$10,000)
Potential Funding Sources: General Funds, EMPG, UASI
Implementation Timeline: Ongoing
Goals Met: 2 and 3
Benefits: High (>$100,000)
